Finding Leaks

How to Find a Water Leak Underground

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 4, 2026 · Updated November 6, 2026 · 5 min read

Short answer: To find a water leak underground, start with the meter: turn off all water and see if it moves. Then close the house main and the irrigation valve one at a time to isolate the leaking line. Walk the pipe's path for green, soggy or sinking spots. To pinpoint it, pros use acoustic listening, line locating and tracer gas.

A buried leak hides in plain sight. In Sarasota's sandy soil, water often drains down instead of pooling, so the yard may look fine. You can narrow the problem down a lot before you make a call. When it's time for exact pinpointing, SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local pro for underground water leak detection in Sarasota.

How to find a water leak underground: 6 steps

Step 1: Confirm there is a leak

Turn off every faucet, appliance and the irrigation system. Read the water meter and note the flow indicator. Use no water for two hours, then read it again. The EPA uses this same two-hour test. If the reading changed, water is leaking somewhere.

Step 2: Close the main shut-off at the house

Find the valve where the water line enters the house and close it. Watch the meter.

  • Meter stops: the leak is inside the house or under the slab.
  • Meter keeps moving: the leak is outside, between the meter and the house, or in a branch line.

Step 3: Shut off the irrigation system

Close the irrigation valve or backflow device, then watch the meter again. If it stops, the leak is in the sprinkler system. Run each zone and look for broken heads or soggy spots.

Step 4: Shut off other branches

Some homes have lines to a pool, a detached garage, an outdoor kitchen or a dock. If each has a valve, close them one at a time. The branch that stops the meter is the one leaking.

Step 5: Walk the pipe's path

Most service lines run in a fairly direct line from the meter to the house entry. Walk it and look for:

  • A strip of grass that's greener or faster-growing
  • Soggy or soft soil in dry weather
  • Small sinkholes or settling
  • Water at the edge of the driveway or a walkway
  • Cracks in concrete near the line
  • A hissing sound near the meter or the house entry

Step 6: Stop before you dig

Don't start digging on a hunch. Florida law requires a call to Sunshine 811 at least two full business days before digging, so gas, power and cable lines can be marked. A wrong guess can mean several holes, or a damaged utility line.

How pros pinpoint underground leaks

Wikipedia lists hydrostatic testing, tracer-gas testing, infrared and acoustic methods as standard ways to find pipeline leaks. Here's what each one does in a yard.

ToolHow it worksBest for
Pressure testA gauge shows whether a closed section loses pressureConfirming which line leaks
Line locatorA transmitter and receiver trace the pipe's path and depthLines with no plans
Ground microphoneAmplifies the sound of water escaping a pressurized pipeMetal and rigid pipe
Tracer gasA safe gas is pushed into the drained line; a sensor finds it at the surfacePlastic pipe and quiet leaks
Infrared cameraShows temperature differences on the surfaceHot lines and shallow leaks

Wikipedia describes tracer-gas leak testing as a nondestructive way to detect leaks, used in industries from construction to manufacturing. In leak detection, it shines where acoustic tools can't hear much.

Why underground leaks are hard to find in Sarasota

  • Sandy soil. Water drains down instead of surfacing.
  • High water table. Near the coast, damp ground is normal, so a wet spot isn't proof.
  • Plastic pipe. Newer lines are quiet, which makes listening harder.
  • Long lines. Some lots have long runs from the street.
  • Hardscape. Driveways and pavers hide the line's path.

Is it your leak or the utility's?

If water rises inside the meter box or bubbles in the street, report it to your utility first. Sarasota County's leak FAQ explains that its staff check reported leaks and decide whether each one is the county's or the customer's. Leaks between the meter and your house are usually yours. Read who is responsible for the water line.

How to prevent underground leaks

  • Keep trees and large shrubs away from the service line's path.
  • Have high water pressure checked and reduced.
  • Replace old polybutylene or galvanized lines before they fail.
  • Mark the line's path after it's been located.
  • Read the meter monthly.

Local note: canal-side yards in Nokomis and bayfront lots in Osprey often stay damp, so rely on the meter, not the soil. In North Port, long lines make step 5 take longer. On Longboat Key, tight lots mean buried lines run close together, so 811 marks are vital.

When should you call a leak detection professional?

Call a pro when:

  • The meter moves with the house main and irrigation closed
  • You can't find any surface clue along the line
  • The leak is under a driveway, pavers or a pool deck
  • You can't find or close your shut-off valves

Frequently asked questions

Can I find an underground leak without special tools?

You can often narrow it to one line with meter tests and valve shut-offs. Finding the exact spot usually takes a pro's tools.

How deep are water service lines in Sarasota?

Depth varies by property and age. Many residential lines are fairly shallow, but a line locator is the only way to know for sure.

What does an underground water leak sound like?

Through a ground microphone it often sounds like a hiss or steady rush. You may hear it yourself near the meter or the house entry if it is large.

Is tracer gas safe for my yard?

The gases used are chosen to be safe. Ask the provider which gas they use and how the test works.
